sentences.text: Backpressure is how a consumer that cannot keep up slows the flow to itself, instead of being flooded or losing work.
A broker pushes messages to consumers without being asked, so a consumer needs a way to say: not so fast.
And whatever it cannot take has to wait somewhere, or be dropped.
Cold-chain monitoring shows both needs.
Sensors in a refrigerated warehouse report forty readings a second.
A reporter writes every reading to a compliance database, which slows down at times.
A live display on the wall only cares about the latest temperatures.
Here, the reporter reads a queue, and acknowledges each reading only once it is written.
The broker stops sending once the reporter holds a hundred unacknowledged readings, and the rest wait on the queue.
The display subscribes directly, with no queue.
When it falls behind, its messaging API drops readings from a small buffer.
The price is that a slow consumer still falls behind.
Backpressure only decides where the backlog waits, or what is thrown away.
The Break it cards show both choices.
Slow the database down, and watch the reporter pause, the broker hold back, and the readings wait on the queue, then arrive.
Slow the display down, and watch it drop the oldest readings, so what it shows stays fresh.
Press Play, and watch the reporter and the display take the same readings in two ways.
Change data capture turns the committed changes in a database into a stream of events, without changing the application that writes to it.
Its usual form reads the database's own transaction log, so every insert, update and delete can reach other systems as it happens.
It is the pattern for systems that cannot, or should not, be modified.
A warehouse's inventory app is a typical case: it is old, it works, and nobody wants to touch it.
It writes every sale and every restock to its own database, and it knows nothing about events.
Yet the shop's search needs current stock figures.
Changing the inventory app to publish events means editing, testing and redeploying a system everyone is wary of.
Polling its tables for changed rows, the simplest form of capture, adds load, and misses what happens between polls, deletes included.
So a connector reads the database's change log, in order, and publishes an event for each change.
The search index keeps its stock figures from those events.
The inventory app is not changed at all.
In the diagram, it has no line to the broker.
There is a price.
The events mirror tables, not business intent: they say a row changed, not why.
Delivery is at least once.
And a database keeps its log only for so long.
The Break it cards show how the connector copes.
Crash it, and watch it carry on from its saved position, with nothing missed.
Then make it lose that position, and see old changes published again, and the search index recognise them by the database's own sequence number, and ignore them.
Press Play, and compare the Inventory App's database with the Search Index: the same stock for every product, a moment apart.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation, or CQRS, separates the part of a system that changes data from the part that answers questions about it.
Commands go to a write model, which checks and records them.
Queries go to a separate read model, shaped for the questions it answers.
The two models can share a database, but in event-driven systems the read model usually has its own store, kept up to date from the write side's events.
The split pays off when writes and reads want different things, and an online shop is a good example.
Checkout writes one order at a time, and every write must be checked.
The account page asks again and again, and wants a ready-made answer: how many orders, and which was the latest.
Put both on one database, and every question adds up a customer's orders on the same tables checkout writes to.
As the shop grows, the questions slow down the orders.
And if that one database is down, nobody can place an order or look one up.
In this scenario, checkout sends commands to the order service, the write side.
Here it accepts every command; a real one would check stock and payment first.
It saves each order, and publishes an event saying an order was placed.
The order history service, the read side, builds its own view from those events: one line per customer, in exactly the shape the account page asks for.
The two sides share nothing but the events.
The price is that the read side is always a little behind the writes, and the product has to decide what users see in between.
Two models are also more to build and run than one, so CQRS pays only where reads and writes really differ.
The Break it cards show both sides.
Slow the read side down, and watch the account page get answers that describe the past, while checkout carries on.
Then take the write side down, and see questions still answered, while commands wait on their queue until it is back.
Press Play, and compare the Order Service and Order History tables: the same orders, kept twice, in two shapes.
Event-carried state transfer is a pattern in which an event carries the state that changed, not just a notice that something changed.
The services that receive it can keep their own copy of that data, and never have to call back the system that owns it.
That matters most for reference data, which many services need and one service owns.
In a shop, the customer service owns every customer's record: their name, and the city they live in.
Shipping needs the city to send each parcel.
Invoicing needs the name and the city to send each bill.
The usual first design is to ask.
When an order arrives, call the customer service, and wait for the answer.
That works, until the customer service is slow, or down.
Then every service that asks is slow, or down, with it.
Here, the customer service publishes the whole record whenever a customer changes.
Shipping keeps its own copy from those events, so an order that carries only a customer id is enough: shipping looks the customer up in its own copy.
Invoicing is left the old way, asking for every single order, so you can compare the two side by side.
The copy has a price.
Every consumer stores one, it is a moment behind the owner, and a service that loses its copy needs a way to get it back.
The Break it cards show both sides.
Stop the customer service, and watch invoicing stall while shipping carries on.
Then restart shipping without its copy, and see what it takes to rebuild it.
Press Play, and compare the Customer Service and Shipping tables as the records arrive.
Event filtering means each consumer receives only the events it wants, and the filtering happens before delivery, not inside the consumer.
On Solace, the first filter is the topic: a subscription says which events to deliver, and the broker sends nothing else.
For a fact that is not in the topic, a selector can filter on a message property instead.
A factory is a natural example.
Sensors on every line, at two sites, report readings several times a second.
One desk wants Berlin's temperatures.
Another wants every reading with severity four or five, from anywhere.
Here, the Berlin desk's queue subscribes to Berlin temperature topics, and the broker never puts anything else on it.
Severity is not in the topic, so the alarm desk's queue takes every reading, and its consumer binds with the selector: severity at least four.
The broker delivers only the matches.
The price is what a selector leaves behind.
Readings it does not match stay on the queue, and nobody will ever take them, so the queue only grows.
The Break it cards show where that leads.
The sensors switch to high resolution, the alarm queue fills its quota, and the broker starts refusing readings, for every subscriber, not just the alarm desk.
Then a typo in the selector stops the alarm desk from binding at all.
Press Play, and watch the number left on the alarm queue.
Event sourcing stores every change to a system's state as an event: appended in order, and never edited or deleted.
The current state is not the record.
It is derived from the events, and can always be rebuilt by replaying them.
Banking is the classic fit, because a ledger must say not just what a balance is, but how it got there.
A simpler design stores the balance and updates it in place, with the history kept to one side, where it can drift from the balance it is meant to explain.
This ledger stores no balances.
A teller sends commands, such as a deposit or a withdrawal.
The ledger checks each one against the current balances, and if it is accepted, records it as an event.
That event is the only thing the ledger ever writes.
Every balance is simply that account's events, added up.
So the history cannot drift from the balance, because the balance is worked out from the history.
And if the ledger loses its balances, it can add the events up again.
The price is that the event history must be complete and durable.
In this demo, the broker's replay log stands in for a real event store.
The Break it cards show why.
Crash the ledger, and watch it rebuild exactly the same balances from the events.
Then lose the event history itself, and see every balance lost with it, because the events were the only record.
Press Play, and watch the Ledger's balances change as the teller's commands arrive.
Event streaming treats events as an unbounded, ordered sequence.
Consumers read the stream in order, each keeping its own position in it, and build state as they go.
A bike-share shows why order and position matter.
Every ride start and every ride end is an event.
To show how many bikes are in use, a counter adds one for each start and takes one away for each end.
That number is only right if the counter has seen every event, in order, from the point its count began.
Miss one, or apply one twice, and the count drifts, with nothing to say so.
Here, a queue holds the ride events in the order they were published, and removes each one only when the counter acknowledges it: that acknowledgement is the counter's position.
Before each acknowledgement, the counter saves a snapshot of its count, together with that position, so after a crash its state and its position still match.
Unlike a log-based streaming platform, a queue does not keep events once they are acknowledged.
To read history again, Solace can keep the stream in a replay log.
The Break it cards show both sides.
Crash the counter, and watch it resume from its snapshot and its position, with the right count.
Then start the city's board late, taking the events direct, with no position and no history, and see its count go wrong from the first ride it never saw start.
Press Play, and compare the counter's count with the number the bikes report.
An exclusive consumer is one consumer that receives every message from a queue, in order, while any others bound to the same queue wait on standby.
If the active one goes away, the broker makes a standby active, and it carries on from where the queue stands.
A ledger is the classic case.
Postings must be applied one at a time, in order.
Apply a refund before the payment it refunds, and the balance is wrong.
So there should be exactly one writer.
But one writer is also one point of failure.
Here, two ledgers bind to one exclusive queue.
The broker makes the first one active, and keeps the second on standby.
The messaging API tells each ledger which it is.
The payments service publishes a posting every half second, and only the active ledger receives them.
The price is the throughput of a single consumer.
And the broker can only see connections: a consumer that hangs while staying connected keeps the queue to itself.
The Break it cards show both sides.
Crash the active ledger, and watch the standby take over within a moment, starting with the postings the crashed one had not acknowledged.
Then make the active ledger hang instead, and see that nothing fails over, and nothing is consumed, until it is stopped.
Press Play, and see which ledger the broker has made active.
Guaranteed delivery means a message, once accepted by the messaging system, is not lost.
The broker stores it before confirming it to the publisher, and deletes it only when the consumer acknowledges it.
Delivery is then at least once, so a consumer must also recognise a message it has already handled.
A loyalty programme shows what is at stake.
Every purchase at the tills earns points.
Lose an award, and a customer is cheated.
Award it twice, and the business pays twice.
Both show up in a customer's balance.
Here, the tills publish each purchase as a guaranteed message, and wait for the broker's receipt saying it was stored.
The points service takes each purchase from its queue, records the award, and only then acknowledges it.
If it restarts before acknowledging, the broker delivers the purchase again, and the points service sees it has already been awarded, and skips it.
The price is work on both sides: the publisher must keep a message until it is confirmed, and the consumer must deal with repeats.
The Break it cards test both promises.
The points service crashes between recording an award and acknowledging it, and the purchase comes back, marked redelivered.
Then the queue stops taking purchases for a while, and the tills keep what was refused, and send it again once the queue is back.
Press Play, and compare the tills' log with the points service's.
A hierarchical topic is an address made of levels, from the general to the specific, with one fact about the event in each level.
Subscribers choose the slice of events they want with wildcards, and the broker does the filtering as it routes.
A retail chain shows why.
Every sale happens in a region, in a store, in a department.
Put those facts into the topic, in a fixed order, and each team can ask for exactly its share: one department everywhere, one region, one store, or everything.
Here, twelve stores in three regions publish four sales a second, each on a topic that names the region, the store and the department.
The electronics team uses a star for the region and the store, so it gets electronics from everywhere.
The EU team names its region, and takes the rest with a greater-than sign.
Audit takes everything.
The stores publish every sale the same way; all the slicing is in the subscriptions.
The price is that the levels become a contract.
Change them, or add one, and subscriptions that counted on the old shape quietly stop matching.
The Break it cards show both ways this goes wrong.
A new team forgets a level, subscribes without any error, and receives nothing.
Then the stores add a level, and the team that counted levels goes quiet, while the teams using greater-than carry on.
Press Play, and compare the three teams' logs.
Point-to-point messaging sends each message to one named destination, usually a queue, and each message is taken by exactly one receiver.
The sender knows where its message goes, and the queue holds it until the receiver is ready.
It fits work that belongs to one known service.
Printing a shipping label is a good example: the order service needs a label printed for every order, by the label printer.
Broadcast the request, and every listener might print one.
Call the printer directly, and a printer that is offline means lost jobs, or an order service stuck waiting and retrying.
Here, the order service sends each label job to the printer's queue, by name.
The label printer is the queue's one reader.
The broker keeps each job on the queue until the printer has taken it and acknowledged it, so no job is lost just because the printer was busy, or away.
If the printer crashed before acknowledging a job, the broker would send it again, so a job may occasionally arrive twice.
The price is coupling by name.
The sender must know the queue, and if another kind of consumer needs the same jobs, it needs a destination of its own.
The Break it cards show both sides.
Take the printer offline, and watch the queue hold the jobs, until it fills and the broker starts refusing new ones.
Then misspell the queue's name in the sender.
Such a message is normally dropped without a word; this broker is set to refuse it back to the sender, so you can see every job bounce.
Press Play, and watch the jobs pass through the queue to the printer.
Publish-subscribe separates the apps that send events from the apps that use them.
A publisher sends each event once, to a topic, without knowing who will receive it.
Every app subscribed to that topic gets its own copy.
An online shop shows why that matters.
Every order placed is news to several teams: shipping must pack it, analytics counts it, and email thanks the customer.
If the shop called each of them in turn, it would have to know them all, wait for each, and change its code whenever a new team wanted the orders.
Here, the shop publishes each order once, on a topic that names the region and the order.
Shipping and email subscribe to every order.
Analytics uses a wildcard to take European orders only.
The broker matches each event against every subscription, and delivers a copy to each match.
A new team can start listening tomorrow, and the shop never changes.
These events are direct messages: the fastest kind, delivered to whoever is subscribed at that moment, and stored for no one.
That is a choice, not part of the pattern.
Publish-subscribe can be guaranteed too, with a queue subscribed to the topic.
The Break it cards show both edges.
Stop shipping for a while, and see the orders it missed while it was away.
Then start a second copy of shipping, and see every order arrive twice, because each subscriber gets its own copy.
Press Play, and open each subscriber's log to see who received what.
Request-reply is a conversation of two messages.
One app sends a request, and waits for a reply addressed back to it.
Because the reply may never come, the wait always has a timeout.
It is the pattern for an app that cannot carry on without an answer.
A supermarket till is a good example: it cannot ring up an item until it knows the price.
Announcing that it needs a price, and hoping, is not enough.
The till needs one answer, to this request, now.
Here, the till publishes a request on a topic that names the item, and waits up to two seconds.
The pricing service, subscribed to that topic, looks the price up and replies.
The till's messaging API made a reply topic for it, and matches each reply to its request.
With the Solace Go API, as here, both are direct messages, and nothing is stored on the way.
Other Solace APIs can also send requests as guaranteed messages, on a queue.
The price, with direct messages, is that both sides must be up at the same moment.
A slow replier slows every asker, and timeouts and retries are the asker's job.
The Break it cards show what that means.
Take the pricing service down, and watch every request time out.
Then make it slower than the till will wait, and see replies arrive after nobody is waiting for them, and get dropped.
Press Play, and compare the till's log with the pricing service's.
